blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Today we take a short trip around Spain. We will learn about daily life, history and languages. Later, we will visit famous places, try the food and go to a spring party.

items.prompt: What do you know about Spain?
What Spanish food have you tried, or what would you like to try?
What time do you usually eat dinner?

blocks.title: Part 1: People and Everyday Life
paragraphs: Most people in Spain live in flats, not houses. Their homes are often small, and the weather is often warm. **So a lot of life happens outside.**
People meet friends in cafés and in the plaza. The plaza is the big square in the middle of a town. **It is like a big living room for everyone.**
In summer, the afternoons are very hot. **So people stay inside in the hottest hours.** In the evening, the air gets cooler. So they go out for the paseo, a slow evening walk.
Families walk through the town and say hello to neighbours. The paseo is not for sport. **It is a way to see your town and your friends.**

images.alt: Families, grandparents and young couples walking slowly along a main street in a Spanish town in the warm evening light, with cafés and flats with balconies

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: People and Everyday Life

items.prompt: Why do many people in Spain go for a walk in the evening?
items.answer: Because the afternoon is very hot, and the evening is cooler.

blocks.title: Part 2: 1492, a Big Year in History
paragraphs: Before 1492, Spain was not one country. **It had several kingdoms.** A kingdom is a country with a king or a queen. The biggest were Castile and Aragon. In the south was Granada, the last kingdom with Muslim rulers.
Isabella was the future queen of Castile, and Ferdinand was the future king of Aragon. **They married, so their kingdoms worked together.**
Isabella and Ferdinand are called the Catholic Monarchs. Monarch is another word for king or queen. **In 1492, they took Granada.** Now they ruled almost all of Spain.
In the same year, they paid for the ships of a sailor called Columbus. He sailed west, and on 12 October 1492, he arrived in America. **That is why 12 October is the national day of Spain.**

images.alt: Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand on horses entering the city of Granada with their army in 1492, with the red Alhambra on the hill

blocks.title: Check: Part 2: 1492, a Big Year in History

items.answer: Isabella and Ferdinand, the Catholic Monarchs.

blocks.title: Part 3: Regions and Languages
paragraphs: Spain has 17 regions, called autonomous communities. **Each one has its own government.** It decides many things for itself, like schools and hospitals.
Why? Long ago, Spain had several kingdoms. **That is why the regions are still different today.** Some even have their own language.

Spanish is spoken all over Spain. People there often call it castellano, **because it first came from Castile.** Around Barcelona, in the north-east, people also speak Catalan. In the Basque Country, in the north, people also speak Basque.
Most languages belong to a language family. **It is a group of languages that grew from one old language.** For example, Spanish and Catalan both grew from Latin.
**But Basque is not in the same family as any other language.** So people who speak only Spanish cannot understand it.

images.alt: A street in Barcelona with Catalan flags on balconies and children walking to school

items.prompt: Why do people in Spain call Spanish castellano?
items.answer: Because it first came from Castile.

blocks.title: Part 4: Famous Places
paragraphs: In Granada, you can see the Alhambra. **It was the palace of the Muslim kings there.** The name is Arabic for *the red one*. Why? The walls are made of red earth.
In Barcelona, there is the Sagrada Família, a very big church by Gaudí. **Building started in 1882, and it is still not finished.**
Why is it so slow? **The church gets no money from the government.** Tickets and gifts from visitors pay for the work. So it can only grow when there is money.

images.alt: The red walls of the Alhambra palace on a hill in Granada, with snowy mountains behind it

items.prompt: Why is the Sagrada Família still not finished?
items.answer: Because only tickets and gifts pay for the work, so the money comes slowly.

blocks.title: Part 5: Food and Meals
paragraphs: **Lunch is the biggest meal of the day, and dinner comes late.** These are the usual times:

- Lunch: about 2 pm
- Dinner: 9 pm or later
Why so late? One reason is the clock. In 1940, the dictator Franco moved the clocks one hour forward. A dictator is a ruler with all the power. **The clocks never went back.**
**So Spain's clocks are ahead of the sun.** In winter, they are about one hour ahead. So dinner at 9 pm is like 8 pm by the sun.
Lunch is also long. Why? **It is the biggest meal, so people eat it slowly.**
After the meal, people stay at the table and talk. There is a word for this time: **sobremesa**, or *over the table*.
A famous lunch dish is paella, from Valencia. It is rice cooked in a wide, flat pan. In Valencia, people call this pan a paella. **So the dish has the same name as the pan.**

images.alt: A big paella with rice in a wide, flat pan on a lunch table, with a family still sitting and talking after the meal

items.prompt: Why does dinner in Spain look late on the clock?
items.answer: Because since 1940, Spain's clocks are ahead of the sun.

blocks.title: Part 6: The Seville Fair and Flamenco
paragraphs: Every spring, Seville has its big fair. **It started as a market for buying and selling farm animals.** Today it is like a small town of colourful tents along long streets.

Each tent is called a caseta. **Most of them belong to families, groups of friends, clubs or companies.** So you usually go in only when the owners invite you. Inside, people eat, drink and dance sevillanas, a happy dance for couples.

Seville is in Andalusia, the home of flamenco. **Flamenco is singing, guitar music and dance together.** The dancer often hits the floor hard with the shoes. So the shoes make music too. The Romani people of Andalusia helped to create flamenco.

images.alt: Women in colourful flamenco dresses dancing sevillanas in pairs in front of striped tents at the Seville Fair

blocks.title: Check: Part 6: The Seville Fair and Flamenco

items.prompt: Who owns most of the tents at the Seville Fair?
items.answer: Families, groups of friends, clubs or companies.

blocks.intro: The evening walk, the late dinner and the word castellano all have a reason.
